title: Campus Ride
summary: Getting off campus shouldn't take longer than the ride.

blocks.text: How might students without a car get off campus quickly, fairly, and safely?
As a team of 3, our goal was to turn one local problem at Livingstone College into a complete two-sided product.

items.title: Product Strategy
items.text: Finding a pricing and trust model that works between classmates.

items.title: Prototyping & Testing
items.text: 76 screens, 13 flows, and a clickable prototype for riders and drivers.

items.title: Iterating with Feedback
items.text: Auditing our first screens and rebuilding them on one system.

blocks.text: Problem: the wait is longer than the ride.

One day I needed to get to Walmart from campus. The shuttle wasn't around, so I ordered an Uber. I waited about 10 minutes to be matched, then about 15 more for the driver to arrive. About 25 minutes of waiting for a 7 minute ride.

frame.alt: A bar for a campus to Walmart trip: 10 minutes matching a driver, 15 minutes with the driver on the way, and 7 minutes riding.

blocks.text: Opportunity: the drivers are already on campus.
Plenty of students have cars and would drive a classmate for a few dollars. They already do it in group chats. What's missing is trust, a fair price, and a way to find each other fast.

items.title: Closer drivers
items.text: A classmate down the hall instead of a driver across town.

items.title: Verified community
items.text: Every rider and driver is a verified student.

items.title: A fair price
items.text: The rider names it, drivers accept or counter.

blocks.text: Introducing Campus Ride: the ride you agree on before you get in.
A mobile app where a rider names a price, nearby student drivers accept or counter, and the rider picks who to ride with.

blocks.text: Campus Ride works on both sides of the ride.
Riders set a price and pick a driver. Students with cars go online between classes and choose the requests they want.

blocks.text: Onboarding to Campus Ride
Proving you belong to the campus before you ever see a driver, for riders and for students who apply to drive.
How students at Livingstone actually get around.
I dug into the campus shuttle, Salisbury's buses and microtransit, ride hailing in small towns, and apps that tried this before.

frame.alt: Collage of transit pages, news articles, a route map, and a group chat ride request.
frame.caption: The shuttle, city transit, ride hailing, and the dorm chat.

blocks.text: In the chat, a student wrote "I will pay someone to take me to Sam's club, it 25 mins away." Someone asked "How much we talking." The answer: "15." Students already name a price for rides. They just do it by hand.

rows: Designated routes and approved activities. When it isn't around, you're on your own. [1]
Two weekday routes, last trips around 7 pm, Saturday service suspended. [2][3]
On demand, Monday to Friday, 6 am to 7 pm, within a set area. [4]
Fewer drivers in small towns. 19% of rural Americans use ride hailing vs 45% urban (Pew). [5]
No trust, no tracking, no payment, no guaranteed reply.

blocks.text: Walmart is 1.9 miles from campus. Sam's Club is 18 miles away in Kannapolis, about 27 minutes by car, which matches the "25 mins" in the chat. [6] Zimride proved closed student networks build trust [7], and inDrive proved riders can name the price [8].
Exploring how a ride should be priced

blocks.text: I designed a system, not just screens.
Every flow for riders and drivers sits on one set of components, so the last screen is as consistent as the first.

blocks.text: Insight 2: The price should never change

items.label: Agree up front
items.text: A suggested $7.00 anchors the rider's own $6.00 offer.

frame.alt: Set your price, with a suggested $7.00 beside a $6.00 offer.

items.label: Carry it through
items.text: Driver Arriving shows the same $6.00, marked Agreed.

frame.alt: Driver arriving, with the agreed $6.00 still on screen.

blocks.text: A ride on every offer isn't possible, yet.
Name your price only works if someone says yes. A low offer, a busy afternoon, or a driver who loses out can break the whole idea.

frame.alt: Campus shuttle, a city bus, ride hailing, group chats, and students with cars.

blocks.title: What happens when nobody accepts my price?

blocks.text: Rider-side recovery
CONSIDERATIONS

blocks.title: How do I help riders raise a fair offer?
blocks.text: When no driver accepts, the rider gets clear ways forward instead of a dead end. Show what nearby riders are offering, with quick picks and "Raise offer" as the main action.

frame.alt: No drivers available, with quick price picks and a raise offer button.

blocks.title: What if they can't pay more?
blocks.text: "Schedule for later" keeps the trip alive instead of ending it.

frame.alt: Schedule for later, so a low offer does not end the trip.

blocks.text: Driver-side negotiation
CONSIDERATIONS

blocks.title: How do drivers decide fast?
blocks.text: The rider's offer, pickup, dropoff, distance, and a 12 second timer on one card.

frame.alt: Incoming request card with the offer, route, and a 12 second timer.

blocks.title: What does losing feel like?
blocks.text: "Rider chose someone else" shows the winning offer, so drivers learn instead of guessing.

frame.alt: Rider chose someone else, with the winning offer visible.

blocks.title: What if they miss it?
blocks.text: "You missed a request" closes the loop and keeps them ready for the next one.

frame.alt: You missed a request, with a way back to the next one.

blocks.text: Trading speed for fairness.
A fixed price would get riders into a car one step faster. I chose fairness and control, and spent the extra design work on making the slow moments (waiting, countering, losing) clear and respectful.

frame.alt: A seesaw with a small speed weight and a larger fairness weight.
frame.caption: Speed against fairness. Fairness is the side I weighted.

blocks.title: A price both sides agreed on is worth one extra tap.

blocks.text: Estimated impact
ESTIMATED, STUDENT FEEDBACK IN PROGRESS

items.text: My wait today: about 10 min to match, plus about 15 min for pickup.
Estimated wait with Campus Ride: 2 to 5 min to get an accepted offer, plus 2 to 5 min pickup by a driver already on campus.

blocks.text: That's an estimated 60% to 84% less waiting. The comparison is (25 minus 10) / 25 and (25 minus 4) / 25. These are assumptions, not measured results. I will replace them with real numbers from student feedback.

blocks.text: What I learned

items.title: The best research was already in our group chat.
items.text: Real behavior beats assumptions.

items.title: Design the "no," not just the "yes."
items.text: Name your price lives or dies on what happens when nobody accepts. Designing "No drivers available" and "Rider chose someone else" made the idea honest.

items.title: Audit before you scale.
items.text: Fixing the first 11 screens was cheap. Fixing all of them would not have been. The system is why the driver side came together fast.

items.title: When a screen keeps moving, it might be two screens.
items.text: Choosing a place and agreeing on a price needed their own screens.
